Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

- **Account:** Active, in good standing

So this isn't a billing or suspension issue — it's most likely a setting or connection issue on the phone itself. Picture messages (MMS) need both cellular service and mobile data working to send.

Let's check a couple of things on your phone. Could you please do the following?

1. **Look at the very top of your screen** (the status bar) and tell me what icons you see — specifically whether you see signal bars, a network type like 5G/4G/LTE, and whether there's an airplane icon.
2. **Try two quick tests:**
   - Can you make a regular phone call?
   - Can you open a web page or use an app that needs internet (with Wi-Fi turned off, if possible)?

Let me know what you find and I'll take it from there.

turns.thought:
Good news — nothing is broken, and your photos are perfectly safe! That's the important part.

That little airplane symbol just means **Airplane Mode is on**. It's a single switch that turns off all the phone's wireless connections at once — cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth. It's very easy to turn on by accident, and it's just as easy to turn back off. It doesn't affect anything stored on your phone.

**Your photos are not lost.** They're saved right on your device. They've just been waiting in your messaging app to be sent — once we get the connection back, they'll go right through to your daughter.

Could you turn Airplane Mode off for me? Here's how:

**On most phones:** Swipe down from the very top of the screen (do it once, and if you only see notifications, swipe down again) to open the full quick-settings panel. Look for the **airplane icon** — it's usually lit up or colored when it's on. Tap it once so it turns gray or dim. That's it.

**If you don't see it there:** Open **Settings**, and there should be an option right near the top labeled **Airplane mode** with a switch next to it — tap the switch to turn it off.

Take your time. Once you've done that, look back at the top of your screen and tell me:
- Is the airplane symbol gone?
- Do you now see signal bars, and any letters like **5G**, **4G**, or **LTE**?

Let me know what you see and we'll go from there. And don't worry — if it's still not working after that, there are several other things we can try.

Two things are going on, and both are fixable:

1. **"Data disabled"** — there's a separate switch for mobile data (internet over the cellular network). It's currently turned off. Picture messages need this to be on, so we definitely want to turn it on.
2. **"No Signal"** — the phone hasn't connected to the network yet. This can sometimes take a few seconds after coming out of Airplane Mode, and if it doesn't, it's usually a simple fix.

Let's start with the data switch, since that's a clear one:

1. Swipe down from the top of the screen again to open that same quick-settings panel.
2. Look for an icon that says **Mobile data** or **Cellular data** (it's often shown as two little up/down arrows). It's likely gray or dim right now since it's off.
3. **Tap it once** to turn it on — it should light up or change color.

turns.thought:
You're not doing anything wrong, and your phone isn't broken — and yes, **France matters a great deal here.** That's actually very likely the whole explanation, and it's good news.

Here's what's happening: when you're outside your home network's coverage area (which you are, being in France), your phone needs your permission to connect to a local partner network. Until you give it that permission, it will show **"No Signal"** — even though nothing is wrong with your phone or your account. That's why the bars didn't come back after you turned Airplane Mode off.

The setting for this is called **Data Roaming**, and it's separate from the Mobile Data switch you already turned on (good job on that — it's on now, which we needed).

**The good news:** I've checked your line, and roaming is already enabled on your account. That means there's nothing to add and no extra charge to worry about. You just need to turn the setting on, on the phone itself.

Here's how to find it:

**On an Android phone:**
1. Open **Settings**
2. Tap **Network & internet** (sometimes called **Connections**)
3. Tap **Mobile network** (or **SIMs**)
4. Look for **Data roaming** (or **Roaming**) and **tap the switch to turn it on**
5. If it asks you to confirm, tap **OK** or **Allow**

**On an iPhone:**
1. Open **Settings**
2. Tap **Cellular**
3. Tap **Cellular Data Options**
4. Turn **Data Roaming** on

If you're not sure which phone you have, look for a small fruit logo on the back — that's an iPhone. Otherwise it's very likely Android.

After you turn it on, **wait a full minute** — connecting to a foreign network can take a bit longer than usual. Then look at the top of your screen again and tell me:

- Do you see **signal bars** now?
- Do you see any letters like **5G**, **4G**, **LTE**, or maybe an **R** or a small triangle (that just means "roaming")?

I know this has been a slog, and I'm sorry it's taken so long. But we've now ruled out the account, the billing, the suspension, and Airplane Mode — and we've found the one thing that explains all of your symptoms at once. I think we're close.

And your photos are still safe on your phone, just waiting to be sent.

One thing stands out to me: you said the phone *told you* mobile data is on, but the top of the screen still says **"Data Disabled."** Those two things should agree. When a phone ignores a setting like that, it's usually because a change is stuck and needs a fresh start to kick in.

**So please try this one step: restart your phone.**

- Tap **Restart** or **Reboot**
- If there's no restart option, choose **Power off**, wait 10 seconds, then press the power button again to turn it back on

This is different from just turning the screen off — it fully reboots the phone. In France on a foreign network, this is genuinely the most common way to make a phone "shake hands" with the local towers. Give it a full two minutes after it comes back on.

turns.thought:
Yes — I'm completely sure. You have my word on it.

**A restart will not delete anything.** Not your photos, not your contacts, not your messages, not your apps. It is exactly what it sounds like: the phone turns all the way off, then all the way on again. That's the entire process.

Here's why your pictures are safe: your photos are saved on storage inside the phone — the same way a photo album sits on a shelf. Turning the phone off and on doesn't touch that shelf. It only restarts the programs that are *running*. Think of it like closing and reopening the messaging app — just with everything at once.

The only thing that ever deletes a photo is someone actively choosing "Delete," or a factory reset (which is a completely different thing, buried deep in settings, and asks you several times to confirm — and I am **not** asking you to do that, and nothing we've discussed would ever trigger it).

Your grandchildren's pictures from the whole trip will be right there in your Photos app when the phone comes back on. I'd stake my job on it.

One thing that will happen: the phone will ask you for your **PIN or unlock code** when it starts back up. That's normal — it always does that after a restart. It's just the phone double-checking it's really you. Use the same code you normally use to unlock it.

So, whenever you're ready:

1. **Hold the power button** (the button on the side or top you use to wake the screen — if a menu doesn't come up, try holding power + volume down together)
2. Tap **Restart** — or **Power off**, wait about 10 seconds, then press power again to turn it back on
3. **Wait a full two minutes** after it restarts before looking at the screen — it needs time to find the French network

Take all the time you need. There's no rush, and I'm right here.

Come back and tell me what you see at the top of the screen — bars, "No Signal," anything at all. And remember: if it's still not working after this, I'll hand you straight over to a technical support specialist who can look at your phone's connection directly. You won't be stuck going through more steps with me.

You're doing great. Go ahead whenever you're ready.
